name: Quantum Fourier transform (statevector)
summary: Apply the QFT gate sequence to a basis, uniform or random state on up to 16 qubits and compare it with the DFT definition.
description:
Applies the quantum Fourier transform, or its inverse, as the real gate sequence (Hadamards, controlled phase rotations and the final qubit reversal) to a state vector on your machine. The input is a computational basis state, the uniform superposition or a seeded random state. The output is compared with an independent reference: the DFT column written straight from its definition for a basis state, the known |0...0> result for the uniform state, and the full DFT matrix product for a random state of up to 10 qubits. The inverse transform is then applied and the round-trip error reported, and the output state is sampled with a seed.

The convention is stated and checked rather than assumed: QFT|j> = (1/sqrt N) sum_k exp(+2 pi i j k / N)|k>, little-endian, so a flipped sign or a reversed bit order would show up as a non-zero deviation. Pure Python: the algorithms extra is used only for seeded sampling.
useCases: Check that the QFT circuit equals the discrete Fourier transform, column by column, to floating-point precision
Show that a basis state transforms to a flat magnitude distribution and the uniform state to |0...0>
Fix the sign and bit-order convention of a QFT before building phase estimation or Shor-type circuits on it

inputs.name: n_qubits
inputs.description: Register size n; the state has N = 2^n amplitudes.

inputs.name: input_state
inputs.description: basis (|basis_index>), uniform ((1/sqrt N) sum_j |j>) or random (seeded complex Gaussian amplitudes, normalised).

inputs.name: basis_index
inputs.description: j for input_state=basis, in [0, 2^n - 1]. Ignored otherwise.

inputs.name: inverse
inputs.description: Apply the inverse transform (negative phases) instead of the forward one.

inputs.name: shots
inputs.description: Measurement samples drawn from the output state.

outputs.name: max_deviation_from_reference
outputs.description: Largest |amplitude difference| between the circuit output and the independent reference named in reference; null when the O(N^2) matrix reference is skipped (random input above 10 qubits).

outputs.name: round_trip_error
outputs.description: Largest |amplitude difference| after applying the opposite transform to the output.

outputs.name: output_norm
outputs.description: Norm of the output state (1 for a unitary transform).

outputs.name: max_magnitude_deviation_from_flat
outputs.description: For a basis-state input: largest deviation of |amplitude| from 1/sqrt N over the output.

outputs.name: output_amplitudes
outputs.description: [real, imaginary] pairs of the output state, listed up to 5 qubits; null above.

outputs.name: counts
outputs.description: Seeded measurement counts of the output, bitstring (most significant qubit first) to count; the eight most probable outcomes are listed in top_outcomes.

changes: First catalog release, wrapping the SDK's existing gate-level QFT with reference comparison, round trip and seeded sampling.

environment.resources: 4 qubits: milliseconds. 16 qubits (65536 amplitudes, forward and inverse, basis-state reference): ~4 s and under 50 MB on a 2024 laptop. The matrix reference for random input costs O(N^2) and is applied only up to 10 qubits (~0.5 s).

example.code:
import json
from ketqat_runner import catalog

record = catalog.run("quantum-fourier-transform@1.0.0", seed=7, n_qubits=4, input_state="basis", basis_index=1, shots=1000)
result = record.result
print(json.dumps({
    "status": record.status,
    "dimension": result["dimension"],
    "matches_dft_column": result["max_deviation_from_reference"] < 1e-9,
    "round_trip_is_identity": result["round_trip_error"] < 1e-9,
    "output_is_flat": result["max_magnitude_deviation_from_flat"] < 1e-9,
    "output_norm": round(result["output_norm"], 9),
}))

verified.platform: macOS-27.0.1-arm64 Python 3.12.12 (maintainer run in a clean virtualenv, test_catalog_examples.py)

sampleResult.summary: 4 qubits, basis state |0001>: the gate-level output equals the DFT column to 12 decimals, every output magnitude is 1/4 (flat), the inverse transform returns the input exactly, and 1000 seeded shots spread over all 16 outcomes.

data.convention: QFT|j> = (1/sqrt(N)) sum_k exp(+2 pi i j k / N)|k>, little-endian (qubit 0 is the least significant bit); the inverse carries the opposite sign
data.reference: DFT column (1/sqrt(N)) exp(+-2 pi i j k / N), written from the definition
data.execution: statevector simulation of the gate sequence (pure Python), seeded sampling of the output

assumptions: Ideal, noiseless gates: Hadamards and controlled phase rotations are applied exactly; no rotation is truncated (the exact, not the approximate, QFT).
Little-endian qubit order (qubit 0 is the least significant bit) and the +2 pi i j k / N sign for the forward transform.
scope: 1 to 16 qubits, forward or inverse transform, basis, uniform or seeded random input.
Deviation from an independent reference, round-trip error, output norm and seeded sampling of the output.
limitations: A statevector simulation in pure Python: 16 qubits is the ceiling, and it says nothing about running on hardware.
Gate counts and depth are not reported, and the approximate QFT (dropping small rotations) is not offered.
For random input above 10 qubits the O(N^2) matrix reference is skipped; only the round-trip error and the norm are checked.
Sampled counts are reproducible for the same seed with the same NumPy version; NumPy does not guarantee identical random streams across versions.
Tested on macOS and Linux only; Windows is untested.

origin.statement: The quantum Fourier transform circuit is due to Coppersmith (1994) and was introduced as the core of Shor's factoring algorithm (1994); the discrete Fourier transform it implements is classical. KetQat wrote this pure-Python gate-level implementation (fourier.py), the DFT reference it is checked against, the validation tests and this catalog entry. KetQat did not invent the method.

validation.description: For every basis state on 1 to 6 qubits, forward and inverse, the circuit output equals the corresponding column of the DFT matrix written from its definition to 1e-12; the product reports the same agreement for a basis input.
QFT followed by its inverse (and the inverse followed by the QFT) returns random states on 1 to 8 qubits to 1e-12, and the product reports a round-trip error below 1e-12 for random input.
The uniform state transforms to |0...0> with every sampled shot landing there, and a basis state transforms to a flat magnitude distribution with |amplitude| = 1/sqrt N to 1e-12.
The example code is executed verbatim in a clean virtual environment with only the algorithms extra installed.
